query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A nanocrystalline refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA), for example a quinary alloy such as W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf, when used as an interlayer between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr, will mitigate thermal expansion mismatch and enhance the radiation and thermal stability of the joint under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Direct bonding of tungsten (W) to CuCrZr tends to suffer from issues related to mismatched thermal expansion coefficients and irradiation‐induced degradation at the interface.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin RHEA interlayer (e.g. W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf) between W and CuCrZr during fabrication.
generation.conditions: High-temperature operation, cyclic thermal loading, and irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactor divertors.
generation.structural_mediator: The RHEA’s nanocrystalline microstructure and its inherent grain stability under irradiation facilitate a graded interface that relieves mechanical stresses.
generation.mechanism: The superior irradiation resistance and thermal stability of the RHEA are expected to dampen the effects of thermal expansion mismatch and reduce defect generation at the interface, thereby improving overall joint durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The interlayer is predicted to reduce residual stresses, mitigate crack formation, and enhance the overall durability of the W/CuCrZr joint under extreme reactor conditions.
generation.baseline: A direct W/CuCrZr joint, which normally exhibits high residual stresses and a propensity for radiation-induced damage due to mismatched thermal expansion.
generation.boundary: The benefits may be limited by potential processing challenges (e.g., achieving defect-free deposition and proper adhesion of the RHEA layer) and scale-up uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of stress reduction and long-term interface stability under reactor conditions is not yet quantified and requires further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W/CuCrZr joined samples: one with an RHEA interlayer (e.g. W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf) and one without. Subject both sets to simulated fusion reactor conditions including high-temperature thermal cycling and ion irradiation.
measurements: Interfacial mechanical strength (shear or tensile tests)
Crack density or defect density at the interface (via microscopy)
Thermal expansion mismatch effects (using thermomechanical analysis)
Microstructural stability (grain size and phase identification before and after testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the RHEA interlayer do not show statistically significant improvements in interface strength, reduced cracking, and better microstructural stability under irradiation and thermal cycling compared to the direct W/CuCrZr joint, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

High thermal stability

The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials [32] . Two main suggested mechanisms are discussed in the literature: (i) defect clusters produced during irradiation can migrate to sub-grain boundaries and form cell structures that lead to small grain formation [32] and (ii) cascades that are larger than the grain size can form stacking faults across the grain breaking it into two separate crystalline structures (observed in FCC material) [33] .
